seo_title: Recoverable Depreciation Explained: How to Get It Back
meta_description: Recoverable depreciation explained: how ACV and RCV payments work, how insurers calculate it, and the steps to get your withheld money back. Read the guide
h1: Recoverable Depreciation Explained: What It Is and How to Get It Back
secondary_keywords: how to get depreciation back from insurance
actual cash value vs replacement cost
excerpt: Learn what recoverable depreciation is, how insurers calculate it, how it differs from non-recoverable depreciation, and the exact steps to collect your withheld claim money.
key_takeaways: Recoverable depreciation is money withheld from an RCV claim until repairs are completed.
Your first check is actual cash value minus your deductible.
Non-recoverable depreciation, common with Texas roof endorsements, is never paid back.
Submit invoices, proof of payment and photos in writing to release the holdback.
Depreciation is negotiable; appraisal can settle disputes over age, life and pricing.
body_html:
Recoverable depreciation is the portion of a replacement cost claim your insurer holds back until repairs are finished. The carrier first pays actual cash value (ACV), which is replacement cost minus depreciation. Once you complete the work and send proof, the withheld recoverable depreciation is released so you receive the full replacement cost, less your deductible.

What is recoverable depreciation?

Depreciation is the loss of value a building component suffers over time because of age, wear and condition. A 12-year-old asphalt roof is worth less than a new one, even though replacing it costs the same as replacing a new roof. Insurers use depreciation to calculate what your damaged property was worth the moment before the loss.

Recoverable depreciation is depreciation you can get back. It exists only when your policy pays on a replacement cost value (RCV) basis. Under an RCV policy, the carrier pays in two stages: an initial ACV check, then a second check for the depreciation it withheld once the repair or replacement is actually done.

Think of it as a holdback, not a reduction. The money is part of your claim value from day one. You simply have to meet the policy conditions to collect it.

The basic recoverable depreciation formula

  • RCV = what it costs today to repair or replace with like kind and quality
  • Depreciation = the value lost to age and condition
  • ACV = RCV minus depreciation
  • Initial payment = ACV minus your deductible
  • Recoverable depreciation = the depreciation released after repairs are complete

Does recoverable depreciation apply to contents?

It can. If your policy includes replacement cost coverage for personal property, the same two-step payment usually applies to furniture, electronics and other contents. The carrier pays the depreciated value first, then releases the holdback once you replace the item and send a receipt. Many standard policies pay contents at ACV unless you bought a replacement cost endorsement, so check your declarations page.

Which claims include recoverable depreciation?

Recoverable depreciation shows up in almost any replacement cost claim: hail and wind roof claims, water damage to flooring and drywall, fire and smoke losses, and commercial property claims written on an RCV form. The larger and older the damaged components, the bigger the holdback tends to be.

You can run your own numbers with our free recoverable depreciation calculator, which shows your ACV payment, holdback and final RCV amount side by side.

Recoverable depreciation example: how the two payments work

Here is an illustrative example. Suppose hail damages your roof, and the carrier's estimate lists a replacement cost of $20,000. The adjuster applies $5,000 in depreciation, and your deductible is $2,000.

Claim componentAmountWhen you receive it
Replacement cost value (RCV)$20,000Total claim value
Depreciation withheld$5,000Held back
Actual cash value (ACV)$15,000Basis for first check
Less deductible-$2,000Never paid by carrier
Initial ACV payment$13,000After the claim is approved
Recoverable depreciation$5,000After repairs are completed and documented
Total paid$18,000RCV minus deductible

Notice that the deductible comes out of the first payment, not the depreciation. If you never finish the repairs, you generally keep only the $13,000 ACV payment and forfeit the $5,000 holdback.

Tip: Read the summary page of your estimate. It usually lists RCV, total depreciation, ACV, deductible and net claim, and often splits depreciation into recoverable and non-recoverable columns.

Recoverable vs non-recoverable depreciation

Not all depreciation comes back. Non-recoverable depreciation is a permanent deduction that you will not receive even after repairs. Whether depreciation is recoverable depends almost entirely on your policy language and endorsements.

FeatureRecoverable depreciationNon-recoverable depreciation
Policy typeReplacement cost (RCV)Actual cash value (ACV) or ACV endorsement
Paid after repairs?Yes, once conditions are metNo
Typical exampleRCV dwelling coverage on a homeRoof on an ACV or roof payment schedule endorsement
Effect on total payoutTemporary holdbackPermanent reduction

Common sources of non-recoverable depreciation

  • ACV-only policies: the policy pays only the depreciated value of damaged property.
  • Roof ACV or payment schedule endorsements: common in Texas, these pay older roofs on a depreciated or percentage basis even when the rest of the house is RCV.
  • Items not replaced: if you choose not to repair a component, the holdback on that item is usually not paid.
  • Missed deadlines: many policies require you to repair within a set time to claim the holdback.

How do insurers calculate depreciation?

Most carrier estimates are written in Xactimate or Symbility, and depreciation is applied line by line. The adjuster enters an age and a life expectancy for each component, and the software calculates a percentage. A roof with a 25-year life that is 10 years old might be depreciated 40 percent, for instance.

Several factors drive the number:

  • Age of the material, often estimated rather than documented
  • Expected useful life, which varies by product and quality grade
  • Condition before the loss, including maintenance and prior repairs
  • Depreciation caps, the maximum percentage an item can be depreciated
  • Whether labor is depreciated, which depends on policy wording and carrier practice

Where depreciation errors hide

Depreciation is one of the most negotiable parts of a claim because it rests on judgment. We regularly see roofs aged older than the permit or purchase records support, life expectancies that are too short for the product installed, and depreciation applied to items like permits, haul-off or contractor overhead that do not wear out. If your roof was replaced eight years ago and the estimate says 15, ask for the basis and send your documentation.

Remember that depreciation is calculated on the carrier's RCV. If the scope is missing items or uses low pricing, your recoverable depreciation will be too small as well. Our guide to signs your insurance claim was underpaid walks through what to look for.

How to get depreciation back from insurance

Recovering withheld depreciation is mostly a paperwork exercise, but the details matter. Follow these steps in order.

  1. Confirm your policy is RCV. Check the declarations page and any roof or wind/hail endorsements so you know which items carry recoverable depreciation.
  2. Note your deadline. Look for the replacement cost condition in your policy. Many set a time limit to complete repairs and notify the carrier, and some allow extensions on request.
  3. Complete the repairs. Replace damaged components with materials of like kind and quality. You can generally hire any qualified contractor.
  4. Gather proof of completion. Collect the final invoice, signed contract, proof of payment, material receipts and before-and-after photos.
  5. Submit a written request. Send everything to your adjuster and ask, in writing, for release of the recoverable depreciation. Keep a copy and note the date.
  6. Follow up. Payments rarely arrive on their own. If the carrier needs more information, provide it quickly and keep a written log.

Our claim documentation checklist lists every record worth keeping from the first inspection through final payment.

What if the repair costs more than the estimate?

Final invoices often exceed the carrier's RCV because of hidden damage, code items or pricing gaps. In that case, ask for a supplement before or along with your depreciation request. A well-supported supplement increases the RCV, which raises the recoverable depreciation too. See supplemental insurance claims explained for how that process works.

What if you spend less?

Most RCV policies pay the lesser of the actual cost to repair or the replacement cost in the estimate. If your contractor charges less than the carrier's RCV, expect the depreciation release to be reduced to what you actually spent.

Why recoverable depreciation gets delayed or denied

Even legitimate depreciation requests stall. The most common causes are avoidable:

  • Incomplete documentation, such as an unsigned invoice or no proof of payment
  • Partial repairs, where only some damaged items were replaced
  • Scope disputes, when the contractor's work does not match the carrier's estimate
  • Missed policy deadlines for completing work or giving notice
  • Self-performed work without receipts or photos to show what was done

If you do repairs yourself, keep every material receipt and take progress photos. Many carriers will reimburse documented materials, but how they handle your own labor varies by policy, so ask your adjuster before you start.

Recoverable depreciation in Texas claims

Texas homeowners deal with depreciation questions more than most because of the state's hail and wind exposure. Spring storms across Dallas, Fort Worth, Austin and Central Texas regularly produce roof claims where depreciation is the largest single deduction on the estimate.

Watch for roof endorsements

Many Texas carriers now attach endorsements that pay roofs on an ACV basis or on a schedule tied to roof age. On those policies, the roof depreciation is generally non-recoverable even if the dwelling is otherwise RCV. Read your policy before a storm so a smaller check is not a surprise.

Prompt payment timelines still apply

The Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542) sets deadlines for insurers to acknowledge, decide and pay claims. How those deadlines apply to a later depreciation request can depend on the facts, so keep dated copies of everything you send. Our Texas claim deadline calculator helps you track key dates. The Texas Department of Insurance also offers consumer help if a carrier is unresponsive. This is general information, not legal advice.

When appraisal helps with depreciation disputes

If you and your carrier disagree about the amount of loss, including how much depreciation applies, most Texas property policies let either side invoke the appraisal clause. Each side names an independent appraiser, and an umpire resolves anything the appraisers cannot agree on.

Appraisal panels commonly set both the RCV and ACV for each item, which settles the depreciation amount directly. That makes appraisal a practical tool when the dispute is about roof age, useful life, pricing or missing scope rather than coverage. Learn more in what is an insurance appraisal.

Next steps to collect your full claim

Recoverable depreciation is real money that belongs to you under a replacement cost policy, but you have to claim it. Confirm your coverage, note your deadline, finish the repairs and submit clean documentation in writing.

Before you accept the numbers, check the depreciation itself. Verify the age and life expectancy on major items, confirm that the RCV includes every damaged component, and push back with evidence when something looks off. If the gap is large, a professional review can help you decide whether a supplement or appraisal is the better path.

faqs.a: Usually not. Most insurers release recoverable depreciation only after you finish repairs and submit proof such as a final invoice, proof of payment and photos. Send a written request to your adjuster with the documents attached and follow up until the payment is issued. Keep a dated record of every submission in case questions come up later.

faqs.q: How long do I have to claim recoverable depreciation?
faqs.a: It depends on your policy. Many replacement cost conditions require repairs to be completed and the carrier notified within a set period after the loss, and some allow extensions if you ask in writing before the deadline. Check the loss settlement section of your policy and confirm the deadline with your adjuster early in the claim.

faqs.q: Can I keep the ACV payment and not repair my roof?
faqs.a: Generally yes, the actual cash value payment is yours to keep, subject to any mortgage company endorsement on the check. However, if you do not complete the repair, you usually give up the recoverable depreciation on that item. Mortgage lenders may also require proof that repairs were made before releasing funds.

faqs.q: Is labor depreciated in an insurance claim?
faqs.a: Some carriers depreciate labor as well as materials, while others depreciate materials only. Whether labor depreciation is permitted depends on your policy wording and the carrier's practice. If labor depreciation appears on your estimate, ask the adjuster to explain the basis and compare it with your policy language.

faqs.q: What happens if my contractor costs less than the estimate?
faqs.a: Most replacement cost policies pay the lesser of the replacement cost in the estimate or the amount you actually spend. If your contractor's final invoice is lower than the carrier's replacement cost figure, the depreciation release is typically reduced so your total payment matches what the repair actually cost.
